claim: Magnetotactic bacteria represent a phylogenetically diverse group including species from Desulfobacterota, several branches of Proteobacteria, and Nitrospira.
source: Magnetotactic bacteria represent a phylogenetically diverse group—including species from Desulfobacterota, several branches of Proteobacteria, and Nitrospira—that use the geomagnetic field to navigate water-saturated sediment (Lefèvre et al., 2014; Delong et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lefèvre et al., 2014 and Delong et al., 1993.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria use the geomagnetic field to navigate water-saturated sediment.
source: Magnetotactic bacteria represent a phylogenetically diverse group—including species from Desulfobacterota, several branches of Proteobacteria, and Nitrospira—that use the geomagnetic field to navigate water-saturated sediment (Lefèvre et al., 2014; Delong et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lefèvre et al., 2014 and Delong et al., 1993.

claim: The dynamics of magnetotaxis are similar across all known bacterial examples.
source: The dynamics of magnetotaxis are similar across all known bacterial examples (Klumpp et al., 2019; Frankel et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klumpp et al., 2019 and Frankel et al., 2007.

claim: A cell or consortium of cells uses flagella to exert a force that is parallel to its permanent magnetic moment.
source: A cell, or consortium of cells (Abreu et al., 2007; Schaible et al., 2024), uses flagella to exert a force that is parallel (Frankel, 1984; Esquivel and De Barros, 1986) to its permanent magnetic moment, which is produced by biologically precipitated inclusions of magnetite or greigite called magnetosomes (Faivre and Schüler, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frankel, 1984 and Esquivel and De Barros, 1986.

claim: The permanent magnetic moment of magnetotactic bacteria is produced by biologically precipitated inclusions of magnetite or greigite called magnetosomes.
source: A cell, or consortium of cells (Abreu et al., 2007; Schaible et al., 2024), uses flagella to exert a force that is parallel (Frankel, 1984; Esquivel and De Barros, 1986) to its permanent magnetic moment, which is produced by biologically precipitated inclusions of magnetite or greigite called magnetosomes (Faivre and Schüler, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faivre and Schüler, 2008.

claim: The magnetic torque on a bacterium turns it like a compass needle to align its magnetic moment with magnetic field lines.
source: The magnetic torque on a bacterium turns it like a compass needle to align its magnetic moment with magnetic field lines.
evidence: The claim is based on established physical principles of magnetic torque and is presented as knowledge.

claim: The alignment motion of magnetotactic bacteria with magnetic field lines is purely physical and requires no behavioral adaptations by the organism.
source: This motion is purely physical and requires no behavioral adaptations by the organism (Frankel, 1984; Esquivel and De Barros, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frankel, 1984 and Esquivel and De Barros, 1986.

claim: As magnetotactic bacteria swim parallel to their magnetic moments, they move along field lines.
source: As magnetotactic bacteria swim parallel to their magnetic moments, they move along field lines.
evidence: The claim follows logically from the previous statements about force direction and magnetic alignment.

claim: The geomagnetic field is rarely parallel to the sediment surface.
source: Because the geomagnetic field is rarely parallel to the sediment surface, magnetotaxis moves bacteria vertically through the sediment, along the dominant chemical gradients that shape microbial life in the top several centimeters of sediment (Blakemore and Frankel, 1981; Lefèvre et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blakemore and Frankel, 1981 and Lefèvre et al., 2014.

claim: Magnetotaxis moves bacteria vertically through the sediment, along the dominant chemical gradients that shape microbial life in the top several centimeters of sediment.
source: Because the geomagnetic field is rarely parallel to the sediment surface, magnetotaxis moves bacteria vertically through the sediment, along the dominant chemical gradients that shape microbial life in the top several centimeters of sediment (Blakemore and Frankel, 1981; Lefèvre et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blakemore and Frankel, 1981 and Lefèvre et al., 2014.

claim: Biased motion allows magnetotactic bacteria to position themselves in changing chemical gradients.
source: This biased motion allows magnetotactic bacteria to position themselves in changing chemical gradients (Bazylinski and Frankel, 2004; Smith et al., 2006) and to shuttle between vertically stratified chemical environments (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bazylinski and Frankel, 2004 and Smith et al., 2006.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria shuttle between vertically stratified chemical environments.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria may be rod-like.
source: Magnetotactic bacteria may be cocoidal (Keim et al., 2007; Acosta-Avalos et al., 2019), rod-like (Spring et al., 1993), or spiral (Bazylinski and Frankel, 2004) with lengths between 1 μm and 20 μm (Esquivel and De Barros, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spring et al., 1993.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria may be spiral.
source: Magnetotactic bacteria may be cocoidal (Keim et al., 2007; Acosta-Avalos et al., 2019), rod-like (Spring et al., 1993), or spiral (Bazylinski and Frankel, 2004) with lengths between 1 μm and 20 μm (Esquivel and De Barros, 1986).

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria have lengths between 1 μm and 20 μm.

claim: Most magnetotactic bacteria species are unicellular.

claim: Swimming speeds of magnetotactic bacteria vary by an order of magnitude, from 12 μm/s to more than 140 μm/s.

claim: There is an optimal combination of magnetic moment, cell size, and swimming speed that maximizes the average speed of magnetotactic bacteria through a pore space.

claim: The average speed of magnetotactic bacteria through an artificial pore space is maximized if the magnetic torque on a bacterium is tuned.
source: This hypothesis was recently independently proposed and tested by Codutti et al., 2024, who found that the average speed of magnetotactic bacteria through an artificial pore space is indeed maximized if the magnetic torque on a bacterium is tuned.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Codutti et al., 2024.

claim: Dehkharghani et al., 2023 examined the effect of obstacle geometry on motion of magnetotactic bacteria through a complex pore space.
source: This analysis is closely related to the work of Dehkharghani et al., 2023, who examined the effect of obstacle geometry on motion of magnetotactic bacteria through a complex pore space.

claim: The speed of magnetotactic bacteria through an artificial pore space is maximized if the distance it swims while aligning with the ambient magnetic field is tuned to the pore size.

claim: A variety of unrelated magnetotactic bacteria from around the world are all optimally efficient navigators of their native pore spaces.
source: Proceeding from a literature review, we then argue that a variety of unrelated magnetotactic bacteria from around the world are all optimally efficient navigators of their native pore spaces.
evidence: The claim is based on a literature review and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multicellular magnetotactic bacteria (MMB) are the only type of bacteria that are known to lack a unicellular stage in their life cycle.
source: MMB are the only type of bacteria that are known to lack a unicellular stage in their life cycle (Keim et al., 2004).

claim: Groups of several tens of non-clonal cells are physically attached together in MMB and coordinate their motion and growth to behave like a single multicellular organism.
source: Groups of several tens of non-clonal cells (Schaible et al., 2024) are physically attached together and coordinate their motion and growth to behave like a single multicellular organism, which is called a consortium.

claim: Individual bacteria are not observed to join or leave existing MMB consortia.
source: Individual bacteria are not observed to join or leave existing consortia.

claim: Each cell in an MMB consortium has its outer surface covered in about 30 flagella.

claim: Cells within an MMB consortium coordinate their activity to exert a net force that is parallel to the consortium's net magnetic moment.
source: Cells within a consortium coordinate their activity to exert a net force that is parallel to the consortium's net magnetic moment (Almeida et al., 2013), which varies among individuals from 3.9 fAm2 to 10.9 fAm2, enabling them to swim at speeds ranging from 45 μm/s to 134 μm/s (Petroff et al., 2022).

claim: The net magnetic moment of MMB consortia varies among individuals from 3.9 fAm2 to 10.9 fAm2.
source: Cells within a consortium coordinate their activity to exert a net force that is parallel to the consortium's net magnetic moment (Almeida et al., 2013), which varies among individuals from 3.9 fAm2 to 10.9 fAm2, enabling them to swim at speeds ranging from 45 μm/s to 134 μm/s (Petroff et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petroff et al., 2022.

claim: MMB consortia swim at speeds ranging from 45 μm/s to 134 μm/s.
source: Cells within a consortium coordinate their activity to exert a net force that is parallel to the consortium's net magnetic moment (Almeida et al., 2013), which varies among individuals from 3.9 fAm2 to 10.9 fAm2, enabling them to swim at speeds ranging from 45 μm/s to 134 μm/s (Petroff et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petroff et al., 2022.

claim: MMB consortia are significantly larger than those studied in previous investigations.
source: As these consortia are significantly larger than those studied in previous investigations (Codutti et al., 2024), it is comparatively simpler to track their motion through a pore space.

claim: When an MMB collides with a surface, the angle at which it escapes can be approximated as uniformly distributed.
source: Additionally, when an MMB collides with a surface, the angle at which it escapes can be approximated as uniformly distributed.

claim: The α-Proteobacteria live at scattering number 0.37 ±0.03.
source: The Desulfobacterota live at scattering numbers of 0.9±0.3 that are somewhat greater than those of the α-Proteobacteria, which live at scattering number 0.37 ±0.03.

claim: It is plausible that the difference in scattering numbers between Desulfobacterota and α-Proteobacteria reflects taxonomic differences in rotational diffusion and cell-wall interactions.

claim: The scattering numbers of magnetotactic bacteria remain within the expected range, suggesting that corrections due to rotational diffusion and cell-wall interactions are of secondary importance.

claim: All magnetotactic bacteria discussed are, to a good approximation, equally and optimally efficient navigators of their native pore spaces.
source: We conclude that all magnetotactic bacteria discussed here are, to a good approximation, equally and optimally efficient navigators of their native pore spaces.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the analysis of literature data.

claim: In an ecologically relevant limit, the efficiency of magnetotaxis is a function of a single dimensionless combination of environmental and phenotypic parameters.
source: We have found that in an ecologically relevant limit, the efficiency of magnetotaxis is a function of a single dimensionless combination of environmental and phenotypic parameters.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The optimal phenotype swims a distance that is similar to the pore radius before aligning with the magnetic field.
source: The optimal phenotype swims a distance that is similar to the pore radius before aligning with the magnetic field.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Swimming a distance similar to the pore radius before aligning causes magnetotactic bacteria to concentrate in the fraction of the pore where escapes are most likely to be found.
source: Doing so causes magnetotactic bacteria to concentrate in the fraction of the pore where escapes are most likely to be found.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Because the efficiency of magnetotaxis depends only on the ratio of phenotypic and environmental parameters, it can be carried out equally well by magnetotactic bacteria with different phenotypes.
source: Because the efficiency of magnetotaxis depends only on the ratio of phenotypic and environmental parameters, it can be carried out equally well by magnetotactic bacteria with different phenotypes.

source: This degeneracy is found to accommodate the natural diversity of magnetotactic bacteria.

claim: The magnitude of the magnetic moment is not determined by the rotational diffusion of the magnetotactic bacteria.
source: The magnitude of the magnetic moment is not determined by the rotational diffusion of the magnetotactic bacteria, which we find to be of secondary importance.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis showing rotational diffusion is secondary.

source: This result suggests that if a bacterium acquires the genes for magnetosome formation and alignment—either de novo or through horizontal gene transfer—then its magnetotactic efficiency is immediately nonzero.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the smooth fitness landscape.

claim: Studies in which the genes for magnetosome formation are added to non-magnetotactic bacteria could provide a strong test of the prediction that magnetotactic efficiency is immediately nonzero.

evidence: The claim is a suggestion for future research based on citations to Kolinko et al., 2014 and Dziuba et al., 2024.

claim: A magnetotactic bacterium can be fast swimming and large only if it produces a very large number of magnetosomes.
source: A magnetotactic bacterium can be fast swimming and large only if it produces a very large number of magnetosomes.

claim: Any species with phenotypic variables laying on the optimal surface is optimally efficient.

claim: The degeneracy in optimal phenotypes allows a species to remain optimally efficient at magnetotaxis while tuning any two of its three phenotypic parameters to other constraints imposed by its ecology.
source: This degeneracy allows a species to remain optimally efficient at magnetotaxis while tuning any two of its three phenotypic parameters to other constraints imposed by its ecology.

claim: The phenotypic flexibility provided by degeneracy gives insight into how magnetotaxis became so widely distributed across bacteria with diverse phylogenies, morphologies, and ecological roles.
source: The phenotypic flexibility provided by this degeneracy gives insight into how magnetotaxis became so widely distributed across bacteria with diverse phylogenies, morphologies, and ecological roles.
